about: The creators turn to the old pair, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, and call on them by all their titles: let them cast lots with maize and tz'ite' seeds and find out whether a person can be carved from wood. The grandmother and the grandfather, the day-keepers, cast the lots and call on the maize, the tz'ite', the day and the shape to speak; the answer comes that it is good: let the people be effigies carved of wood. At once the wooden people are made. They multiply and have daughters and sons, and they talk, but they have no heart and no mind and do not remember the Heart of Sky who made them. Their faces are dry, their legs and hands have no strength, they have no blood. The man's flesh is tz'ite' wood, the woman's is reed pith. So the Heart of Sky sends a flood upon them: a great resin comes down from the sky, creatures with strange names come to gouge out their eyes, cut off their heads, eat their flesh and break their bones, and the earth grows dark under a black rain that falls by day and by night. Then the animals come in, and the people's own things, their griddles, plates and pots, their dogs and their grindstones, begin to speak against them.

sentences.t: “Chi cutun ibi, Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Vtiu, camul Alom, camul Ꜭaholom,
sentences.l: “Let-it-appear your-name, Hunahpu Opossum, Hunahpu Coyote, twice Child-Bearer, twice Son-Begetter,
sentences.i: “Let your name be shown, Hunahpu Opossum, Hunahpu Coyote, twice the Mother of children, twice the Father of sons,
sentences.n: The creators' speech to the old pair goes on from the end of the last part, and the old pair are now called by a long roll of titles. Chi cutun ibi 'let your name appear': chi of wishing + cutun 'appear, be shown', the root of vcutunizaxic 'its being shown' in the preamble; i- before bi 'name' is 'your (pl.)', the two elders spoken to together (Brasseur 'make your name known'). Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q (= ꜭ); the toggle shows k'utun, as the pilot's uk'utunisaxik. Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Vtiu are names from the preamble's litany (in Vtiu the ß-ligature is read ti, as Brasseur). camul 'twice' (ca- 'two' + mul 'time'): the preamble has camul Iyom, camul Mamom; here the elders are given the creator pair's own titles, Alom, Ꜭaholom.

sentences.t: Nimac, Nima Ꜯyꜩ, ahcuval, ahyamanic, ahchut, ahꜩalam,
sentences.l: Great-ones(?), Great Coati, he-of-jade(?), he-of-gems(?), he-of-the-chisel(?), he-of-planks(?),
sentences.i: Nimac, Great Coati, worker in jade, jeweller, carver, carpenter,
sentences.n: Nimac, Nima Ꜯyꜩ: the manuscript has nimac nima / ꜯyꜩ across a line end, where the preamble's litany has Zaqui Nimac Ꜯyꜩ 'White Great Coati'. nimac is nim 'great' with the plural -ac, nima is 'great': the pair may be a slip of repetition, nimac written and then nima again before ꜯyꜩ. Brasseur divides Nim-Ak 'Great Peccary' and Nima-Tzyiz, as other editors divide the pilot's nimac. Nimac is left untranslated in i. Four titles with ah- 'he of, one who' follow, the names of crafts. Their senses are inferred from Brasseur's French ('the one of the emerald, the jeweller, the engraver, the architect') and his notes, and all four are uncertain: cuval 'jade, precious stone' (Brasseur ahqual; the manuscript writes cuval with v), yamanic 'gems, jewellery', chut 'awl, chisel', ꜩalam 'plank, board', so that ahꜩalam is a worker in boards. The toggle respells their letters as written.

sentences.t: Ah Raxa Lac, Ah Raxa Ꜩel, ahꜫol, Ahtoltecat, Ratit Ꜫih, Ratit Zac, quix vꜭhaxic rumal caꜯac, cabit.
sentences.l: He-of Green Plate, He-of Green Bowl, he-of-resin, He-of-Toltecat, Grandmother of-Day, Grandmother of-Light, you-shall-be-called by our-built, our-shaped.
sentences.i: He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Bowl, He of the Resin, the Toltec, Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light: so you shall be called by those we build, those we shape.
sentences.n: Ah Raxa Lac, Ah Raxa Ꜩel are titles from the preamble. The pilot printed Laꜫ, but here the manuscript has a plain c, and the c is printed; the toggle shows laq 'plate', as in the pilot. ahꜫol 'he of the resin': ꜫol is resin or gum (Brasseur 'master of the resin'); Ximénez's 3-shaped tresillo is read ꜫ, as Brasseur's g. The word comes back in the flood below, nima ꜫol 'a great resin'. Ahtoltecat is joined as the manuscript writes it and capitalised as a name (Brasseur ah-Toltecat): Toltecat is the Nahuatl word for a Toltec, one of the people of the old city of Tula, and in Nahuatl it also meant a skilled craftsman, which fits the crafts before it. Ratit Ꜫih, Ratit Zac 'Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light', as in the last part (the looped letter in Ratit read t). quix vꜭhaxic 'you (all) shall be called': quix 'you all (shall)' with vꜭhaxic, the passive of ꜭha 'say' that in xe vꜭhaxic means 'they were told'. caꜯac, cabit 'our built, our shaped' are the beings the creators mean to make, as with the animals in the last part.

sentences.t: Chi mala chi ixim, chi ꜩite;
sentences.l: Let-(you)-cast-lots(?) with maize, with tz'ite';
sentences.i: Cast the lots with the maize, with the tz'ite';
sentences.n: The elders are asked to divine. chi mala: chi of wishing + mala, taken as 'cast lots, sort the seeds'; the sense is inferred from Brasseur's French ('make your passes') and from xmalic 'what was cast' a few lines on. Brasseur divides Ch'y mala, which may hide i- 'you (all)' in chi; l shows the 'you' in brackets, as with chi byih in the last part. The second and third chi are the preposition 'with, at'. ixim is maize. ꜩite is the tz'ite', the coral tree, whose hard red seeds the diviners mix and count out with grains of maize to cast the lot (Brasseur's note). No comma is visible on Ximénez's ligature in this word, so it is printed with ꜩ although it is a tz' word; the toggle shows tz'ite'.

sentences.t: xa chi banatahic, xa pu chel apanoc chi cahah, chi ca cotah puch vchi, vvach che?” xe vꜭhaxic e ahꜫih.
sentences.l: only shall-it-be-done, only also shall-it-come-out later(?) that we-carve(?), that we sculpt(?) also its-mouth, its-face of-wood?” they-were-told the day-keepers.
sentences.i: will it be done, will it come about that we carve, that we sculpt its mouth and its face in wood?” So the day-keepers were told.
sentences.n: The question the lots are to answer. chi banatahic 'shall it be done': chi + banatah, the passive of ban 'do, make' (as xbanatah 'it was done' in the first part), + -ic. chel 'let it come out' (el 'go out'); apanoc is not otherwise known, and 'later, in time' is a guess. chi cahah, chi ca cotah are a couplet of woodworking with ca- 'we': cahah is taken as ca- + ah 'carve', the root of aham che 'carved of wood' and xahaxic 'he was carved' below, and cotah as 'sculpt, gouge', following Brasseur's French ('that we work and sculpt'). Both senses are inferred. In cotah Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q (= ꜭ), so the toggle respells the letters. vchi, vvach che 'its mouth, its face of wood': the new person is to have a wooden face. xe vꜭhaxic e ahꜫih 'the day-keepers were told': e marks the plural. One of the two ahꜫih of this part has a blot between the h and the q-shaped letter, which is read ꜫ.

sentences.t: Cate puch vcahic vꜫihiloxic ri xmalic chi ixim, chi ꜩite.
sentences.l: Then also its-casting-down(?), its-being-honoured(?) the was-cast(?) with maize, with tz'ite'.
sentences.i: Then came the casting and the honouring of what was cast with the maize, with the tz'ite'.
sentences.n: The divination itself. vcahic 'its casting down' is taken from cah 'go down' (Brasseur 'to cast (the lot)'; his note on cahizabal below gives kah 'go down, bring down'); Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has k (that is q), and the toggle respells it as written. vꜫihiloxic 'its being honoured' is the passive noun of ꜫihila 'honour' from the last part, built on ꜫih 'day', and may here mean the day-keeper's greeting or reckoning of the days (Brasseur 'to greet'); the sense is uncertain. Ximénez's q-shaped letter is read ꜫ, as Brasseur's g. xmalic 'what was cast(?)': x- + mal, the verb of chi mala above, + -ic.

sentences.t: “Ꜫih, bit!” xeꜭha cu ri hun atit, hun mama chiquech.
sentences.l: “Day, shape!” they-said then the one grandmother, one grandfather to-them.
sentences.i: “Day! Shape!” said a grandmother and a grandfather to them.
sentences.n: The words spoken over the lots: ꜫih 'day, sun' and bit 'shape', the day of the calendar and the shaping of the new person (Brasseur 'Sun and Creature!'); Ꜫih is the q-shaped letter read ꜫ. The same four, ixim, ꜩite, ꜫih, bit, are spoken to together below. hun atit, hun mama 'one grandmother, one grandfather': hun 'one' serves as 'a'; the looped letter in atit is read t, as in Ratit. xeꜭha 'they said' and chiquech 'to them' are both plural, and who is spoken to is not said: perhaps the seeds, perhaps the creators.

sentences.t: Are ri mama, are ahꜩite, Xpiyacoc vbi; are cu ri atit, ahꜫih, ahbit, Chiracan Xmucane vbi.
sentences.l: This-is the grandfather, this-is he-of-tz'ite', Xpiyacoc his-name; this-is then the grandmother, day-keeper, shaper, Chiracan Xmucane her-name.
sentences.i: The grandfather was the one of the tz'ite', Xpiyacoc by name; the grandmother was the day-keeper, the shaper, Chiracan Xmucane by name.
sentences.n: The two diviners are named. ahꜩite 'he of the tz'ite'', the one who casts with the seeds (ah- 'he of'). ahꜫih 'day-keeper' and ahbit 'shaper', the titles the pair had together in the last part, belong here to the grandmother. The grandfather is Xpiyacoc and the grandmother Xmucane, as in the preamble. Chiracan is an epithet of Xmucane met only here (Brasseur Chirakan); its meaning is unknown. vbi 'his name, her name': v- does not mark gender.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cut, ta xqui tiquiba ꜫih: “Xa chu culu, xa pu chu rico;
sentences.l: They-said then, as they planted(?) day: “Only let-it-come-together(?), only also let-it-find;
sentences.i: Then they spoke, as they set out the days: “Let it come together, let it be found;
sentences.n: xqui tiquiba ꜫih 'they planted the day': tiquiba 'plant, begin' is the verb of xchicatiquiba 'we shall plant' in the preamble, and planting the day is taken as laying out the count of days for the reading; this is inferred (Brasseur 'when the sun stood still'). The manuscript keeps qu in tiquiba, where Brasseur has q. Xa chu culu, xa pu chu rico: in the last part Ximénez wrote Xuculu as one word before xa pu chu rico, and it was printed so; here the same words are written apart, xa chu culu, and that Xuculu is probably this phrase. chu 'let it' (ch- + v- 'it'); culu is taken as 'meet, come together' (Brasseur 'it is time to take counsel'), which is a guess, and the toggle respells it as written. rico 'find', as in the last part.

sentences.t: cha byih, ca ta ca xiquin, caꜭhauic, caꜩihon tah,
sentences.l: say, tell, it-hears(?) our-ear, it-speaks, it-talks let,
sentences.i: speak, tell it, so that our ears may hear; let it speak, let it talk,
sentences.n: The day-keepers call on the lot to speak. cha byih 'say, tell': cha 'say' and byih, the doubtful spelling of bih 'say' met in the last part, printed as there. ca ta ca xiquin is taken as ca- (ongoing) + ta 'hear' and ca xiquin 'our ear' (xiquin 'ear'), 'our ear hears' (Brasseur 'that we may hear'); the division and the sense are inferred. caꜭhauic, caꜩihon 'it speaks, it talks': ca- marks the ongoing action, and the speaker is the lot itself; tah, the particle of wishing, makes them 'let it speak, let it talk'. ꜩihon 'talk' is the verb of ꜩih 'word'; ꜭh is the colonial spelling of ch'.

sentences.t: xa chu culu ri che chahauaxic, chi cotox puch cumal Ahꜯac, Ahbit, ve are ꜩucul, cool, ta chavaxoc, ta zaquiroc.”
sentences.l: only let-it-come-together(?) the wood shall-be-carved(?), shall-be-sculpted(?) also by-them He-who-builds, He-who-shapes, whether this-is provider, sustainer, when will-be-sown, when will-dawn.”
sentences.i: let it come together whether the wood shall be carved, shall be sculpted by the Builder and the Shaper, whether this will be the provider, the sustainer, when there is sowing, when there is dawn.”
sentences.n: The question of the lots again. chahauaxic 'shall be carved' is taken as ch- (shall) + ah 'carve' with a passive ending, and chi cotox 'shall be sculpted' as chi + cot with the passive -ox; both forms and senses are inferred from Brasseur's French ('whether the wood must be carpentered and sculpted'). In cotox Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q. cumal 'by them'; Ahꜯac, Ahbit are the creators' titles of the last part. ve 'if, whether' (Brasseur 'si'). ꜩucul, cool 'provider, sustainer', and ta chavaxoc, ta zaquiroc 'when there is sowing, when there is dawn', repeat the creators' wish; chavaxoc is written with v here, where the pilot spells chauaxoc.

sentences.t: “At ixim, at ꜩite, at ꜫih, at bit, cat choconic, cat taquentah,” xꜭha chire ixim, ꜩite, ꜫih, bit.
sentences.l: “You maize, you tz'ite', you day, you shape, you-shall-be-of-use(?), you-shall-be-commanded(?),” said to-him/her maize, tz'ite', day, shape.
sentences.i: “You maize, you tz'ite', you day, you shape, be of use, be at our bidding,” so one said to the maize, the tz'ite', the day and the shape.
sentences.n: at 'you (one)' and cat 'you (one) shall': each of the four is spoken to as one. choconic and taquentah are uncertain. choconic is taken as chokon 'serve, be of use' and taquentah as 'be sent, be commanded' (taq 'send'), both inferred; Brasseur took the pair instead as the call of mating ('unite, couple'), with a strong sense, he says, in the original. In choconic Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (= ꜫ); in taquentah he keeps qu where Brasseur has q; the toggle respells the letters. xꜭha 'said' is singular, and the speaker is not named; chire 'to him, to her' is singular too, the four taken as one.

sentences.t: “Cat quix la vloc, at Vꜭux Cah; ma ca hizah vchi, vvach Tepeu, Ꜫucumaꜩ.”
sentences.l: “You-shall be-ashamed(?) la(?) hither, you Heart of-Sky; not you-bring-down(?) its-mouth, its-face Sovereign, Quetzal-Serpent.”
sentences.i: “Come hither and blush, Heart of Sky; do not bring low the mouth and the face of Tepeu and Q'ucumatz.”
sentences.n: A doubtful line. Cat quix la vloc: the manuscript writes quixla, divided as Brasseur divides it (qix la), and there is a blot on the c of vloc. cat is 'you (one) shall', so quix cannot be the plural 'you all (shall)' here; it is taken as a verb, perhaps 'be ashamed' (Brasseur 'blush') or 'prick with thorns' (his note: 'come and prick yourself, draw blood with thorns', after the custom of offering one's blood). la is unexplained. vloc 'hither, this way'. ma ca hizah: the manuscript writes macahizah, and the division is uncertain (Brasseur m'aqahizah). It is read as ma 'not' with a verb 'bring down' from cah 'go down' + -iza 'make' (as in cahizabal below), and a- 'you': 'do not bring down'. To bring down someone's mouth and face is to shame him. All of this is inferred, and the toggle respells the letters as written.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha, ta xqui bih cut vzuculiquil: “Vꜩ are chuxoc ri i poy, aham che, chi ꜭhauic, chi ꜩihon bala chuvach vleu.”
sentences.l: They-said, as they told then its-truth: “Good this let-it-be the your effigy, carved wood, that it-speak, that it-talk bala(?) on-the-face-of earth.”
sentences.i: They spoke, and told the truth of it: “It is good: let it be your effigies carved of wood, that will speak, that will talk on the face of the earth.”
sentences.n: The lots answer, through the diviners. vzuculiquil 'its truth, its rightness' (zucul 'straight, true' + -il; Brasseur 'the truth'). xqui bih 'they told', the verb bih 'say'. ri i poy 'your effigies': i- 'your (pl.)' with poy 'effigy, doll', written apart (Brasseur ri y poy); the effigies belong to the creators. aham che 'carved wood': aham is the perfect participle of ah 'carve' (compare ꜯibam 'written' in the preamble), 'carved of wood'. chi ꜭhauic, chi ꜩihon 'that they speak, that they talk'. bala is unexplained (Brasseur 'at their ease') and is left out of i.

sentences.t: “Ta chuxoc,” xeꜭha cut, ta xqui bih.
sentences.l: “So let-it-be,” they-said then, as they said-it.
sentences.i: “So be it,” they said, as they spoke.
sentences.n: Ta chuxoc 'so let it be', the formula of the creators' decisions (ch- + ux 'become' + -oc). xqui bih 'they said it': bih 'say' with xqui 'they (did it)'.

sentences.t: Huzuc xbanic poy, aham che; xe vinac vachinic, xe vinac ꜩihonic puch; are vinaquil vvach vleu.
sentences.l: At-once was-made effigy, carved wood; they person bore-fruit, they person talked also; this-is people of-the-face of-earth.
sentences.i: At once the effigies were made, carved of wood; they came forth as people, they talked as people; these were the people of the face of the earth.
sentences.n: Huzuc 'at once', as when the earth rose. xbanic 'it was made': x- with no person prefix and the ending -ic, a passive of ban. In the manuscript the a is closed and looks like u (xbunic); Brasseur's x-banic is followed. xe vinac vachinic, xe vinac ꜩihonic: vinac 'person' stands inside the verb phrase, 'they bore fruit as people, they talked as people'. vachin 'bear fruit, show itself', on vach 'face, fruit', is the word used in the last part of the animals' speech, which never took shape; here it does. vinaquil 'people, peopling' (vinac + -il), as vvinaquil huyub 'the mountain's people' in the last part; the manuscript has qu here as Brasseur.

sentences.t: Xe vxic, xe poꜫic, xe mealanic, xe ꜭaholanic ri poy, aham che;
sentences.l: They-came-to-be, they-multiplied, they-had-daughters, they-had-sons the effigy, carved wood;
sentences.i: They came to be, they multiplied, they had daughters, they had sons, the effigies carved of wood;
sentences.n: xe vxic 'they came to be' (ux 'become', as xuxic in the first part). xe poꜫic 'they multiplied': Ximénez's q-shaped letter is read ꜫ, as Brasseur's g (pogic). In the last part the blessing on the deer and birds (qui poco, quix poc) was printed with plain c, and the root is probably the same. mealanic 'have daughters' and ꜭaholanic 'have sons' are verbs made from meal 'a man's daughter' and ꜭahol 'a man's son' (the ꜭahol of Ꜭaholom): the children are named as a father names them.

sentences.t: ma cu habi qui ꜭux, ma pu habi qui naoh; mavi natal cahꜯac, cahbit.
sentences.l: not then there-was their heart, nor also there-was their mind; not remembered their-builders, their-shapers.
sentences.i: But they had no heart and no mind; their builders, their shapers were not remembered.
sentences.n: ma cu habi, ma pu habi 'there was no ..., nor': habi is the existential of mahabi 'there is not' in the preamble, here split by cu 'then' and pu 'also'. qui ꜭux 'their heart' and qui naoh 'their mind' are what the creators used in planning the world. natal 'remembered', from nat 'remember' (xqui natah 'they remembered' below) with the ending -al; the exact form is uncertain. cahꜯac, cahbit 'their builders, their shapers', as in the last part.

sentences.t: Xa loc xe binic, xe chacanic.
sentences.l: Only aimlessly(?) they-walked, they-went-on-all-fours(?).
sentences.i: They only wandered without purpose, going on all fours.
sentences.n: xa loc 'only, to no purpose' follows Brasseur ('without aim'), who prints xalog; the sense is inferred, and the toggle respells the letters as written. binic 'walk', as in the last part. chacanic is glossed by Brasseur 'go on all fours', like the animals; it is uncertain.

sentences.t: Mavi xqui natah chic ri Vꜭux Cah; quehe cut xe pah chi vi.
sentences.l: Not they-remembered any-more the Heart of-Sky; thus then they-fell(?) at-that(?).
sentences.i: They no longer remembered the Heart of Sky, and so they fell.
sentences.n: xqui natah 'they remembered', the transitive verb behind natal above, with chic 'any more'. xe pah is taken as 'they fell, they were brought low', following Brasseur's French ('they fell'); the sense is inferred. chi vi is what the manuscript has (chivi), read as chi 'at' + vi 'there': 'by this, there'. Brasseur prints chiri 'there'.

sentences.t: Xa vtihtobexic, xa pu vvababexic chi vinac.
sentences.l: Only its-being-tried, only also its-being-attempted(?) at people.
sentences.i: It was only a trial, only an attempt at people.
sentences.n: vtihtobexic 'its being tried', the word of the second attempt in the last part (the ß-ligature read ti). vvababexic is written vvaba-/bexic across a line end, and the letters are printed as seen; Brasseur's text is lost in the OCR here, and his French has 'attempt'. It is taken as the pair of vtihtobexic, with the same ending -exic, but the root is not known and the word is uncertain. chi vinac 'at people'.

sentences.t: Que ꜭhau nabec, xa chaquih qui vach; mana zonol cacan, qui ꜫab;
sentences.l: They-spoke at-first, only dry their face; not firm(?) their-legs, their hands;
sentences.i: They spoke at first, but their faces were dry; there was no strength in their legs, in their hands;
sentences.n: Que ꜭhau 'they spoke': que is c- (ongoing) + e 'they', as in xa que vachelahic in the last part, here with ꜭhau 'speak'. nabec 'at first'. chaquih 'dry'. mana 'not', a form of ma. zonol is unexplained, and 'firm' is a guess from Brasseur's 'without consistency'. cacan 'their legs, their feet': c- (qui- before a vowel) + acan 'leg, foot'; Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has k (c'akan; his k is q), and the toggle shows kaqan. qui ꜫab 'their hands': here the 3-shaped tresillo is read ꜫ (Brasseur gab), as in chuꜫab 'on the arm of' in the last part; the same word is written with plain c, qui cab, two lines on.

sentences.t: ma habi qui quiquel, qui comahil; ma habi qui ticoval, qui cabchiyal;
sentences.l: not there-was their blood, their substance(?); not there-was their moisture(?), their fat(?);
sentences.i: they had no blood and no substance, no moisture and no fat;
sentences.n: Four things the wooden people lacked, in two pairs. quiquel 'blood' is certain. comahil, ticoval and cabchiyal are not otherwise known, and their senses ('substance', 'moisture', 'fat') follow Brasseur's French and are guesses. In ticoval the ß-ligature is read ti, as Brasseur; in cabchiyal Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (= ꜫ), and the toggle respells the letters as written.

sentences.t: chaquih coꜩ ꜭoh qui vach; ca pichipoh cacan, qui cab; ca ieioh qui tiohil.
sentences.l: dry coꜩ(?) ꜭoh(?) their face; are-pichipoh(?) their-legs, their hands; are-ieioh(?) their flesh.
sentences.i: their faces were dry and shrunken; their legs and their hands were withered; their flesh was slack.
sentences.n: coꜩ ꜭoh is unexplained (Brasseur cotz qoh, 'dried cheeks'); this ꜭoh is not the puma of the last part. ca marks the ongoing state, 'they are'. pichipoh is clear in the manuscript, but Brasseur's text is lost in the OCR here (his French has 'arid'); its meaning is unknown, and 'withered' in i is only a guess. qui cab 'their hands' is the ꜫab of the line before, written with plain c (Brasseur gab); the toggle shows q'ab'. ca ieioh is written caie-/ioh across a line end (Brasseur ca yeyoh, 'languishing'); the word is unknown, and 'slack' is a guess. tiohil 'flesh', the word used of the animals in the last part.

sentences.t: Quehe cut mavi xe nau chi vi chuvach Ꜯacol, Bitol, alai quech, ꜭuxlaai quech.
sentences.l: Thus then not they-thought at-that(?) before Builder, Shaper, bearer of-them, cherisher of-them.
sentences.i: So they had no thought before the Builder and the Shaper, the one who bore them, the one who cherished them.
sentences.n: xe nau 'they thought, they understood': nau is the verb of naoh 'mind', as in xe nauic below. chi vi again, as two lines before (Brasseur's French adds 'to raise their heads'). alai quech, ꜭuxlaai quech 'their bearer, their cherisher' are the titles alay rech, ꜭuxlaay rech of the preamble, spelled here with i. quech here is 'theirs, of them' (qui- 'their' before a vowel + ech), not 'ours' as in the last part; the toggle shows kech.

sentences.t: E nabe ꜩaꜩ chi vinac xe vxic varal chuvach vleu.
sentences.l: They first many at people they-came-to-be here on-the-face-of earth.
sentences.i: These were the first people who came to be here in great numbers on the face of the earth.
sentences.n: E 'they (are)': the plural marker stands as the subject. ꜩaꜩ 'many, thick, dense' (Brasseur 'in great number'). chi vinac 'of people'. xe vxic 'they came to be', as above.

sentences.t: Cate cut qui quyzic chic, qui mayxic, qui cutuxic puch; xe camizax chic poy, aham che.
sentences.l: Then then their-end(?) now, their-ruin(?), their-destruction(?) also; they-were-killed also effigy, carved wood.
sentences.i: Then came their end, their ruin and their destruction: the effigies carved of wood were put to death in their turn.
sentences.n: Ximénez marks a new paragraph here with a capital, where Brasseur begins his chapter three. qui quyzic is a doubtful reading: the letter after qui looks like a g, but it is followed by u and is read qu. Brasseur reads qizic 'their end', which would be ꜭiz 'finish' (chiꜭiz in the preamble) with -ic; 'end' follows him and is uncertain, and the toggle respells the letters as written. qui mayxic and qui cutuxic are not otherwise known; 'ruin' and 'destruction' follow Brasseur's French. In cutuxic Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (= ꜫ). xe camizax 'they were killed': camiza 'kill' (cam 'die' + -iza 'make') with the passive -x. chic 'also, in their turn': the animals too were given over to be killed.

sentences.t: Ta xnohix qui butic rumal Vꜭux Cah; nima butic xbanic, xpe pa qui vi ri e poy, e aham che.
sentences.l: Then was-conceived(?) their flooding by Heart of-Sky; great flood was-made, it-came on their head the they effigy, they carved wood.
sentences.i: Then their flooding was conceived by the Heart of Sky; a great flood was made, and it came down on the heads of the effigies, of those carved of wood.
sentences.n: xnohix 'it was conceived': x- + nohih 'conceive, think out' (as xqui nohih in the last part) with the passive -ix. The sense is inferred, for Brasseur took the root as noh 'fill' ('the waters were swollen'). butic 'flood, flooding' (Brasseur 'inundation'); qui butic 'their flooding'. xbanic 'it was made', as above. pa qui vi 'on their heads': vi 'head, top', as in chuvi 'on top of'. e poy, e aham che: e marks both as plural.

sentences.t: Ꜩite vtiohil ri achih, ta xahaxic rumal Ꜯacol, Bitol; ixoc zibac cut vtiohil ixoc xrah oquic rumal Ꜯacol, Bitol.
sentences.l: Tz'ite' his-flesh the man, when he-was-carved by Builder, Shaper; woman: reed-pith(?) then her-flesh woman, it-wanted entering by Builder, Shaper.
sentences.i: Tz'ite' wood was the flesh of the man, when he was carved by the Builder and the Shaper; and reed pith was the flesh of the woman: so the Builder and the Shaper willed it to go into her.
sentences.n: What the wooden people were made of. The man's flesh was tz'ite', the wood of the tree whose seeds were cast above (no comma on the ligature here either; the toggle shows tz'ite'). achih 'man'. xahaxic 'he was carved': ah 'carve', the root of aham che, with the passive -ax and -ic. zibac is, in a colonial vocabulary cited by Brasseur, the pith of a small reed of which mats are made (another gives sassafras); 'reed pith' follows him and is uncertain. ixoc 'woman' stands twice, before and after. xrah oquic 'it wanted entering': xrah is x- + r- 'it' + ah 'want', active and singular, as in the last part, with the wanted act following as a noun (oquic 'entering', from oc 'enter'); with rumal Ꜯacol, Bitol 'by the Builder, Shaper' it is the creators' will. The manuscript has the r of xrah; Brasseur prints xah oquic.

sentences.t: Mavi xe nauic, ma pu xeꜭhauic chuvach cahꜯac, cahbit, banol que, vinaquirizay quech.
sentences.l: Not they-thought, nor also they-spoke before their-builders, their-shapers, maker of-them, bringer-into-being of-them.
sentences.i: They did not think, they did not speak before their builders and their shapers, the one who made them, the one who brought them into being.
sentences.n: xe nauic 'they thought': the intransitive form of nau with -ic. banol 'maker', an agent noun of ban 'make', like Ꜯacol and Bitol; vinaquirizay 'one who brings into being': vinaquir 'come into being' + -iza 'make' + the agent ending -y (as ziquiy 'caller' in the last part). que and quech are both 'of them' here.

sentences.t: Quehe cut qui camizaxic; xe butic; xpe nima ꜫol chila chicah.
sentences.l: Thus then their-being-killed; they-were-flooded; came great resin there from-sky.
sentences.i: And so they were put to death: they were flooded, and a great resin came down from the sky.
sentences.n: qui camizaxic 'their being killed', the passive noun of camiza. xe butic 'they were flooded', butic 'flood' as a verb. ꜫol 'resin, gum', the word of the title ahꜫol above: the 3-shaped tresillo is read ꜫ (Brasseur gol), and Brasseur's French has 'a thick resin'. chila chicah 'there from the sky'.

sentences.t: Xecotcovach vbi xcotin vloc vbac qui vach; xe pe Camaloꜩ, xcupin vla qui holom;
sentences.l: Xecotcovach his-name gouged(?) hither the-bone(?) of-their face; they-came Camalotz, cut-off(?) hither their head;
sentences.i: One named Xecotcovach came and gouged out their eyes; Camalotz came and cut off their heads;
sentences.n: The creatures that destroy the wooden people, each with its own work. Brasseur takes them as birds of prey whose names were no longer in use; nothing more is known of what they were. Xecotcovach vbi 'Xecotcovach by name'. xcotin 'gouged' is taken from cot, the verb of chi ca cotah 'that we sculpt' above, and Ximénez again writes plain c where Brasseur has q. vbac qui vach 'the bone of their face', perhaps their eyeballs (vach is also 'eye'): Brasseur 'tore out their eyes from the sockets'. The senses are inferred. vloc and vla 'hither, coming': the creature comes to do its work. xe pe 'they came' is plural though Camaloꜩ is one, printed as written (Brasseur x-e pe). xcupin 'cut off' is inferred from Brasseur's French. holom 'head'.

sentences.t: xpe Coꜩbalam, xtio qui tiohil; xpe Tucumbalam, xtucuuic, xquichouic qui baquil, qui bochil;
sentences.l: came Cotzbalam, ate their flesh; came Tucumbalam, were-broken(?), were-ground(?) their bones, their sinews(?);
sentences.i: Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; Tucumbalam came, and their bones and their sinews were broken and ground;
sentences.n: Coꜩbalam and Tucumbalam both end in balam 'jaguar'. xtio 'ate, bit into': ti 'bite, eat meat', the ß-ligature read ti as Brasseur, with -o, the ending of a transitive verb; the 'it' prefix is not written. Tucumbalam is written with the looped letter that looks like h (hucumbalam), read t as in Ratit. xtucuuic is printed with the letters as seen (Brasseur x-tukuvic). xtucuuic and xquichouic end in -ic, not in a transitive ending, and are taken as passives with the bones as their subject; 'broken' and 'ground' follow Brasseur's French and are inferred. baquil 'bone' (bac + -il); bochil is unknown, and 'sinews' is a guess (Brasseur 'cartilage').

sentences.t: xcahixic, xmuchulixic qui baquil, cahizabal qui vach.
sentences.l: were-brought-down(?), were-crumbled(?) their bones, means-of-bringing-down their face.
sentences.i: their bones were cast down and crumbled, to bring their faces low.
sentences.n: xcahixic and xmuchulixic are passives in -ix: cah 'go down' (as vcahic above) and much 'crumble, pound'; Brasseur has 'reduced to powder and scattered'. Both senses are inferred. The manuscript has qui baquil 'their bones' here a second time, which Brasseur leaves out. cahizabal 'means of bringing down': cah + -iza 'make' + -bal, the noun of means (Brasseur's note: 'to humble, to lower their faces'); to bring down a face is to humble it, as in ma ca hizah above. In xcahixic and cahizabal Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q and k; the toggle respells the letters as written.

sentences.t: Rumal mavi qui nauic chuvach qui chuch, chuvach puch qui cahau, ri Vꜭux Cah, Huracan vbi; cumal xꜫecumaric vvach vleu, xticaric ꜫecal hab, ꜫihil hab, acabal hab.
sentences.l: Because not their-thinking before their mother, before also their father, the Heart of-Sky, Huracan his-name; because-of-them darkened its-face earth, began black rain, day rain, night rain.
sentences.i: Because they had not thought before their mother and before their father, the Heart of Sky, whose name is Huracan, the face of the earth was darkened because of them, and a black rain began, rain by day, rain by night.
sentences.n: rumal 'because' introduces the cause, and cumal 'by them, because of them' brings in the result. qui nauic 'their thinking', the noun of xe nauic above. qui chuch, qui cahau 'their mother, their father': the Heart of Sky is mother and father, as the creator is in the preamble. Before the second chuvach Ximénez blotted out a word; nothing can be read under it. xꜫecumaric 'it grew dark': ꜫecum 'darkness' + -ar 'become'. Ximénez's q-shaped letter is read ꜫ, as Brasseur's g, though the pilot printed the same word queꜫum with qu at the start. xticaric 'it began', the verb of vticaribal 'its planting, its beginning' in the preamble (ß read ti). ꜫecal, ꜫihil, acabal 'black, of day, of night', each with hab 'rain': rain at every hour. acabal is aꜫab 'night' + -al, written with plain c (Brasseur agabal); the toggle shows aq'ab'al.

sentences.t: Xoc vla chuti chicop, nima chicop; xcut qui vach rumal che, abah.
sentences.l: Entered hither small animal, great animal; were-struck(?) their face by tree, stone.
sentences.i: The small animals and the great came in, and their faces were struck by the trees and the stones.
sentences.n: Xoc vla 'they came in': oc 'enter' with vla 'hither, coming', as with xcupin vla above. chuti chicop, nima chicop 'small animals, great animals', the phrase of the animals' charge in the last part. xcut is taken as a passive, x- with no person prefix and the agent brought in by rumal 'by'. Its sense is uncertain: Brasseur's French says the people were 'maltreated in the face' by wood and stone, and his note gives the literal sense 'showed their faces', from the root of cutun 'appear' at the start of this part; 'struck' is a guess from the context, and the toggle respells the letters as written. Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q.

sentences.t: Xꜭhauic ronohel qui quebal, qui xot, qui lac, qui boh, qui ꜩi, qui caa, haruh pala ronohel; xcute qui vach.
sentences.l: Spoke all their household-things(?), their griddles, their plates, their pots, their dogs, their grindstones(?), however-many all; struck(?) their face.
sentences.i: All their household things spoke, their griddles, their plates, their pots, their dogs, their grindstones, all of them, as many as there were; and they struck at their faces.
sentences.n: The household turns on its owners; their speeches begin the next part. Xꜭhauic 'it spoke', singular, with ronohel 'all' as its subject. qui quebal is not otherwise known: Brasseur's French has 'all that had served them', so it is taken as the household things in general, which the list then names; this is inferred. xot 'griddle', the clay comal for tortillas; lac 'plate', written with plain c as in Ah Raxa Lac above; boh 'pot' (Brasseur 'griddles, plates, pots'). ꜩi 'dog', with no comma on the ligature; the toggle shows tz'i'. Between qui quebal and qui xot the images pass over two blank leaves; nothing is missing. qui caa is uncertain: the letter after qui is a c with a flourish, and Brasseur prints qui aq 'their turkeys' (his 'hens'). caa 'grindstone', the metate on which maize is ground, is read here because the grindstones speak in the next part; the toggle respells the letters as written. haruh pala 'however many' (Brasseur 'as many as there were'). xcute is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has xcuhe, with the looped letter read t, and Brasseur prints x-qutu. It is taken as the verb of xcut above, now with the household as its subject, and its sense is uncertain.
